strengths: Clear problem formulation: recasting zero-shot coordination as a Hidden-Utility Markov Game and framing partner adaptation as in-context learning is a sensible and well-motivated reframing that distinguishes partner generalization from task generalization in prior ICL-RL work (e.g., DPT, Algorithm Distillation).

Comprehensive evaluation on the standard ZSC-Eval protocol across five Overcooked layouts, with sensible metrics (BR-prox plus episode reward), proper held-out evaluation partner selection via DPP sampling, and a comparison suite covering population-based (MEP, HSP), fine-tuning (HSP-ft), and contextual meta-RL (HSP-meta) baselines.

Rare and valuable human-agent collaboration study (36 participants, blind color-coded pairing, randomized order) showing COOT is preferred as a collaborator, complementing the policy-based benchmarks with both quantitative returns and qualitative feedback.

Useful analyses: adaptation curves over 50 episodes, partner-swap experiments quantifying episodes-to-recover (avg. 3.67), and ablations on context length and trajectory shuffling that yield genuine insights (temporal structure is critical, unlike findings in simpler navigation settings).

Good reproducibility practices: complete hyperparameter tables, dataset construction details, hardware/training time, inference cost comparison, algorithm pseudocode, and a reproducibility statement with released scripts and configuration files.

The paper honestly reports where COOT is not dominant (e.g., HSP beats COOT's reward on Coord. Ring; HSP slightly better in Asymm. Adv.), discusses limitations (structured environment, no mutual adaptation modeling), and discloses LLM usage and human-study ethics/consent procedures.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single environment family (Overcooked layouts from ZSC-Eval). Given that the central claim is a general framework for in-context partner adaptation, evidence from at least one additional coordination domain (e.g., Hanabi, as in few-shot coordination work cited) would be needed to support generality claims.

The method is a fairly direct application of the DPT recipe (supervised pretraining of a GPT-2-style transformer on best-response actions conditioned on trajectory contexts) to the coordination setting; the technical novelty beyond the reframing is modest, and no theoretical grounding or analysis of when in-context best-response prediction should generalize is provided.

Some baseline conclusions rest on potentially weak implementations: HSP-meta (a PEARL-inspired encoder built atop HSP) underperforming vanilla HSP is surprising, and the paper's post-hoc explanations (reconstruction loss misalignment, noisy latents) are speculative. Stronger meta-adaptive baselines (e.g., Varibad-style, cited but not compared) or PECAN, the most related few-shot coordination method, are absent.

Effect sizes are mixed: COOT's BR-prox advantage is small or absent in several layouts (e.g., Coord. Ring 0.47 vs HSP 0.49), and the headline gains come mainly from Multi-recipe and Bothway Coord. Results appear to be single training runs reported with rollout-level std (50 rollouts) rather than across training seeds, making robustness of the reported differences unclear.

The human study is only in one layout (Coord. Ring) with 36 participants, no statistical significance testing is reported, and two weaker baselines were excluded post hoc; outlier trimming (top/bottom 10%) without pre-registration weakens the evidential strength of the human-evaluation claims.

COOT is trained per layout (~19h each), so it does not address cross-layout or cross-task transfer, which somewhat narrows the practical significance of 'in-context' adaptation compared to methods that generalize across environments.

strengths: The core idea of framing zero-shot partner coordination as in-context learning over interaction histories is clean and well-motivated, and the HU-MG formulation cleanly separates the problem from prior task-generalization ICL work (Section 4.1).

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: benchmark comparisons across five Overcooked layouts with BR-prox and reward metrics, a controlled user study (36 participants, blinded agent identities, consent and compensation documented in Appendix D), adaptation-speed and partner-swap (non-stationarity) analyses, and ablations on context length and trajectory shuffling.

The paper is transparent about design details: full hyperparameters (Table 6), dataset configuration (Table 5), hardware/training cost (~300 GPU hours), inference-time comparisons, and a reproducibility statement with released scripts.

The ablations are informative rather than decorative, e.g., showing that step-wise trajectory shuffling (beneficial for DPT in Dark-Room) hurts in Overcooked, providing genuine insight into when temporal structure matters for ICL in MARL.
Limitations are honestly discussed in the conclusion, including the structured-environment scope and lack of explicit mutual adaptation modeling.
weaknesses: The claim of generalization to 'unseen partners' is weaker than presented: training and evaluation policies are drawn from the same finite candidate pool of 36 ZSC-Eval checkpoints (Algorithm 1 selects top-M for Πtrain and removes them from Π0; Algorithm 2 samples Πeval from the remainder). These are disjoint but drawn from the same family of hidden-reward-trained policies, so COOT may be exploiting a fairly narrow, predictable partner distribution rather than truly generalizing; no experiments with genuinely out-of-distribution partner types (e.g., human-like or architecturally different policies) beyond the single-layout human study are provided.

Results in Table 1 do not fully support the abstract's claim that COOT 'consistently outperforms' baselines: in Coord. Ring, HSP achieves higher reward (41.10 vs 38.30) and ties on BR-prox, and in Asymm. Adv. HSP/HSP-ft slightly exceed COOT. The advantage is concentrated in coordination-heavy layouts, and the framing oversells the breadth of the win.

Limited methodological novelty: COOT is essentially a Decision-Pretrained Transformer (Lee et al., 2023) repurposed from task generalization to partner adaptation, with a supervised best-response prediction loss. The architectural choice (GPT-2 with 4 layers, 2 heads, 128 embedding) and the training objective are presented without analysis of why this would produce in-context adaptation versus simple context memorization of the 36-partner pool.

Potentially important experimental details are unexplained or suspect: the shared global reward r_t is included in the context but it is unclear how informative it is about the partner's hidden utility; MEP's near-total collapse in Counter Circ (1.89 vs 21.37 for HSP) is reported without discussion; the variance in HSP (±10.03 in Coord. Ring) suggests checkpoint sensitivity that is not analyzed.

The HSP-meta baseline (the most relevant adaptive comparator) underperforms vanilla HSP, but the paper's explanation (reconstruction loss misalignment) is speculative post-hoc reasoning; a better-tuned contextual baseline would substantially strengthen the central claim that in-context conditioning is the right mechanism.

The human study is limited to a single layout, uses outlier removal of top/bottom 10% of participants (a filtering step that could favor the adaptive method), and reports subjective ratings on an ad-hoc 1–6 two-dimension scale whose psychometric properties are not justified; no IRB or ethics-board approval is mentioned, only 'standard ethical guidelines.'

The fairness of comparisons is muddled: MEP/HSP are framed as upper bounds using dense reward shaping, yet they are simultaneously treated as baselines COOT should beat; the contribution would be clearer with a strict sparse-reward comparison throughout.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: shifting in-context learning from task generalization to partner generalization in zero-shot coordination, which is a distinction the authors frame convincingly against prior DPT/ICL-RL work (Sections 2, 4.1).

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: five Overcooked layouts, five baselines (BC, MEP, HSP, HSP-ft, HSP-meta), the ZSC-Eval protocol with BR-prox and average reward metrics, 50 rollouts per partner, and analysis of adaptation speed (Fig. 3) and non-stationary partners (Table 4).

A 36-participant human study with informed consent, blinded agent identities, randomized ordering, quantitative returns/ratings, preference rankings, and qualitative feedback (Tables 2, 3, 12) provides evidence beyond synthetic policy partners, which most ZSC papers lack.

The fine-tuning comparison (Table 11, Appendix C.3) and the HSP-meta analysis (Appendix C.4) provide genuine insight into why gradient-based and latent-context adaptation fail here, rather than merely reporting that baselines lose.

Reproducibility support is strong: dataset construction parameters (Table 5), full hyperparameters (Table 6), hardware/training time, inference-time comparison, algorithms, and a code/scripts reproducibility statement.
The authors are candid about limitations, including evaluation in a structured environment and the lack of mutual-adaptation modeling (Section 6).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is modest: the core method is a small GPT-2 trained with supervised cross-entropy to imitate precomputed best-response actions given trajectory contexts, closely following the DPT recipe (Lee et al., 2023); the HU-MG formulation and partner generation are largely inherited from HSP (Yu et al., 2023) and ZSC-Eval (Wang et al., 2024). The contribution is primarily empirical and combinational rather than methodological.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: all results are on Overcooked, and the 'unseen' evaluation partners are drawn from the same candidate pool of event-biased HSP/MEP policies as training partners (Appendix B.1). Generalization to genuinely out-of-distribution partner types is not demonstrated, and the authors themselves note deployment partners must be 'modeled using this set of reward functions' — a significant scope restriction for the generality claims in the abstract.

The claim that COOT 'consistently outperforms' baselines is stronger than the data: in Coord. Ring, HSP actually achieves higher mean reward (41.10 vs. 38.30), and in Asymm. Adv. the differences are within noise. The advantage is real but concentrated in specific layouts.

The human study lacks statistical analysis (no significance tests or confidence intervals beyond quartiles), uses a small sample (n=36), excludes the top and bottom 10% of scores post hoc, and only tests one layout; the appendix instructions (Fig. 9) inconsistently describe '3 layouts' and '7 different agents' versus the reported 4-agent, 1-layout design.
An obvious related baseline, PECAN (Lou et al., 2023), which is explicitly context-aware ZSC and cited in Related Work, is not compared against empirically, weakening the comparative case.

Practicality concerns are underexplored: training requires ~19 GPU-hours per layout and a curated population of pretrained best-response policies per layout, and COOT performs with an empty context in its first episode (i.e., degrades to BC behavior), yet the cold-start penalty is not quantified separately.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem (few-shot adaptation to unseen partners in ad-hoc teamwork) and positions it clearly against prior context-based methods (PACE, LIAM, PLASTIC, GAMMA, HSP-meta) that rely on compressed latent contexts.

The technical approach is simple but well-designed: cross-episode context conditioning on full interaction histories, with independently sampled query states to force genuine partner inference rather than trajectory completion; the appendix (Sec. G) gives a thoughtful analysis distinguishing CooT from behavior cloning, including an error-accumulation argument (O(1/sqrt(K)) regret vs. compounding error) supported empirically by Figure 2.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: two benchmarks (Overcooked with 5 layouts, GRF), BR-prox and return metrics under the ZSC-Eval protocol, many strong baselines (BC/BC-RNN, MEP, HSP, HSP-ft, HSP-meta, PACE, PLASTIC, GAMMA, sparse-reward controls), sanity checks that training and evaluation populations are disjoint, sensitivity analyses over evaluation partner sets, and ablations on context length, shuffling, partner diversity, and data scale.

The IRB-approved human study (36 participants, double-blind, randomized order, qualitative coding with manual verification) provides evidence beyond simulated partners, including perceived adaptability and non-stationary partner-switching experiments.

Reproducibility is strong: detailed hyperparameters, dataset construction, hardware, training time (~19h/seed per layout), licensing of codebases, and honest treatment of baseline fairness (e.g., explaining why CooT's use of HSP population data is a conservative comparison, and the sparse-reward control in Table 26).

Limitations are discussed honestly (no explicit communication, simulation-focused, no-prior protocol costs, degradation with stale context), and the impact statement and human-study consent materials are appropriate.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the architecture and training objective are a fairly direct application of Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) ideas to the partner-adaptation setting; the main contributions are the HU-MG framing, cross-episode context design, and empirical evidence rather than a new algorithmic principle.

The headline claim that CooT 'consistently outperforms' baselines is somewhat overstated: in Table 1 CooT trails HSP-fit/HSP in Coord. Ring return (38.3 vs. 41.5) and Asymm. Adv. return (129.5 vs. 134.0/133.5), and bolding results 'within the best method's std' is a generous reporting convention; per-layout gains are layout-dependent as the authors themselves acknowledge.
Only 3 training seeds are used for the main comparisons, and some layout-level differences have overlapping standard deviations, which limits statistical confidence in per-layout claims.

Evaluation partners are generated from the same family of event-based hidden-utility reward functions as training partners, so out-of-distribution generalization is only partially tested; the human study covers a single layout, so the claim of suitability for 'real-world human-AI collaboration' is supported but narrowly.

The context-length result (performance degrading beyond 5 episodes) is not fully explained, and the Jensen-Shannon divergence sanity check (0.3314 vs. 0.2976) has a subtle interpretation that could be presented more rigorously.
Scalability beyond two agents (Overcooked) or three attackers (GRF) and to substantially larger teams is left open; GRF evaluation is limited to a single scenario.

strengths: The core idea—treating partner adaptation as an in-context learning task by training a transformer to predict best-response actions conditioned on full cross-episode interaction histories—is clearly articulated and well-motivated relative to compressed-latent context methods (PACE, PECAN, LIAM, PEARL-style encoders).

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: five Overcooked layouts plus a GRF scenario, a broad set of baselines (BC, BC-RNN, MEP, HSP, HSP-ft, HSP-meta, PACE, GAMMA, PLASTIC, sparse-reward variants), three training seeds, and standardized metrics (return and BR-prox from ZSC-Eval).

The pipeline sanity checks are commendable: the training/evaluation population overlap analysis (Figure 6, JS-divergence comparison), sensitivity of results to evaluation partner selection (Table 14), a systematic HSP-meta hyperparameter search (Figure 5, Table 8), and dense-vs-sparse reward controls (Table 26) address common objections to ad-hoc teamwork evaluations.

A human study with 36 participants, IRB review, randomized and double-blind agent ordering, qualitative analysis with manual verification of LLM-assisted coding, and published consent materials represents a strong commitment to validating real-world claims.

The ablations (context length, temporal shuffling, dataset scale, partner switching) are informative, and the honest limitations discussion (cold-start protocol, no communication, benchmark-only settings) is appropriate.
The distinction between COOT and behavior cloning is carefully argued in Appendix G, addressing the most obvious criticism of the method.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the architecture and training procedure are a direct application of Decision-Pretrained Transformers (Lee et al., 2023) to a new objective (partner-conditioned best-response prediction). The conceptual contribution is a reframing ('partner as task') rather than a new algorithmic mechanism, and the paper offers no theory of its own—the regret argument in Appendix G borrows Corollary 6.2 of Lee et al. under assumptions (e.g., near-linear dynamics) that do not obviously hold in Overcooked.

The claim that COOT 'consistently outperforms' all baselines is overstated. In Table 1, HSP and HSP-ft match or exceed COOT on Coord. Ring return (41.10 vs 38.30) and on Asymm. Adv. (134.01 vs 129.48), with overlapping confidence intervals in several cells; the advantage is concentrated in specific coordination-heavy layouts.

The evaluation partner distribution is narrow: both training (36) and evaluation (10–15) partners come from the same generative process of event-based hidden rewards built on HSP/MEP/MAPPO checkpoints. Generalization to genuinely out-of-distribution behaviors is tested only in a single-layout human study (36 participants, one layout, four agents), so the claim of 'reliable real-world human-AI collaboration' exceeds the evidence.

Several baseline results raise implementation concerns: PACE underperforming vanilla HSP by large margins (e.g., 4.43±9.02 vs 29.35 in Coord. Ring Multi-recipe, with a suspiciously large std) and HSP-meta performing below HSP suggest the adapted context-based baselines may not have been tuned as effectively as the headline method, even with the reported hyperparameter search.
GRF experiments are thin: a single scenario (3vs1 with Keeper), a reduced baseline set, and no per-partner breakdown, which weakens the scalability claim beyond two-agent discrete grid-worlds.

The fragility of the context design is acknowledged but not resolved: performance degrades beyond 5 context episodes, and chunk-wise shuffling only marginally improves over no augmentation, leaving open questions about robustness of the learned adaptation mechanism.

Reproducibility is partially supported (detailed hyperparameters, compute estimates of ~800 GPU hours, public frameworks), but no explicit code or dataset release is stated, and the reliance on curated pretrained checkpoints from ZSC-Eval makes exact replication dependent on artifacts not clearly committed to release.

Presentation has minor issues: notation introduced then redefined (π_w vs π_p_i), occasional typos and inconsistent capitalization (CooT/COOT), and the partner-switch analysis (Table 4) is limited to three hand-picked preference pairs in one layout.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framing: recasting ad-hoc teamwork as in-context partner adaptation, treating each partner behavior as a 'task' whose best response is inferred from cross-episode interaction histories. The distinction from task-centric ICL (DPT) is articulated clearly.

Comprehensive and careful experimental evaluation: two benchmarks (Overcooked with five layouts including a multi-recipe variant, and GRF), a broad baseline suite (BC/BC-RNN, HSP, MEP, HSP-ft, HSP-meta, PACE, plus GAMMA, PLASTIC, and sparse-reward variants in the appendix), three training seeds, and the standard ZSC-Eval protocol with BR-prox and BR-div/DPP partner selection.

Strong ablation and analysis section: context length (with a sensible discussion of stale history), temporal shuffling (chunk-wise vs. step-wise), dataset-scale and partner-diversity scaling, partner-switch experiments quantifying adaptation speed, and adaptation curves over episodes.

Notable pipeline-sanity checks rarely seen in this area: macro analysis breaking partner-BR pairs across train/eval populations, JS-divergence micro analysis, and sensitivity of results to alternative evaluation partner sets — these directly address the risk that gains come from memorizing training partners.

A well-designed human study (36 participants, IRB review, randomized double-blind agent order, qualitative coding with manual verification) that complements the RL-based evaluations and demonstrates real-world relevance for human-AI coordination.

Above-average reproducibility: full hyperparameter tables, dataset configuration, hardware, training/inference costs (~800 GPU hours), reliance on open-source codebases, and honest discussion of limitations and LLM usage.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate. The core contribution is applying a DPT-style supervised in-context objective to partner adaptation; the architecture is a small GPT-2 and the training objective is plain cross-entropy on best-response actions. The conceptual leap over prior context-based AHT methods (PECAN, LIAM, TAGET, concurrent Weis et al.) is real but incremental.

Some baseline results raise concern about implementation/tuning quality: HSP-meta underperforms vanilla HSP on nearly every layout, and PACE shows pathological variance (4.43±9.02 on Coord. Ring Multi-recipe, std exceeding the mean). The authors' hyperparameter sweep partially addresses HSP-meta, but hypotheses about the failure mechanisms are speculative rather than diagnosed empirically.

COOT does not uniformly dominate: HSP matches or exceeds it in return on Coord. Ring and Asymm. Adv., and BC is nearly on par on Bothway Coord. (BR-prox 0.94 vs 0.96). The headline advantage is driven largely by multi-recipe and coordination-heavy layouts, which the authors acknowledge, but the abstract-level claim of consistent superiority is somewhat overstated.

The GRF evaluation (Table 2) uses only a subset of baselines (no PACE, HSP-meta, or context-based methods), limiting the strength of the scalability claim; scaling to larger teams is deferred as open work.

The theoretical justification in Appendix G informally applies Corollary 6.2 of Lee et al. (2023) to argue regret decreases as O(1/sqrt(K)); the assumptions behind this transfer (e.g., coverage of the partner by the training distribution, behavior policy conditions) are not verified, so this argument is suggestive rather than rigorous.

The human study covers a single layout, reports ratings without statistical significance testing, and the qualitative coding sample sizes are small (e.g., N=9 adaptation mentions for COOT), so human-study conclusions should be read as preliminary.

Minor presentation issues: some inconsistencies in figure/table labeling (e.g., duplicate '(e)' labels in Figure 3), typos, and citations to not-yet-existing works (arXiv:2602.16301, dated 2026) that should be cleaned up.
